Investigating the effect of mono di carboxylic acids as hydrogen bond donor on solvation of copper in choline chloride-based deep eutectic solvents

## A B S T R A C T Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are green alternatives to highly acidic solvents or ionic liquids (ILs). The flexible complexation properties of eutectic solvents open their scope as a prospective dissolution medium for metal extraction. The present study investigates the range of monocarboxylic acids-choline chloride (Monocarboxy A-ChCl) and dicarboxylic acid-choline chloride (Dicarboxy A-ChCl) DESs as solvent media for copper oxide dissolution with a discussion on physical properties and their effect on dissolution. Thermal stability, freezing point, Kamlet Taft parameter, density, and viscosity of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs were experimentally determined. The density of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs follows the trend: FA-ChCl < Acetic A-ChCl < OA-ChCl < MA-ChCl < CA-ChCl. The viscosity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be lesser than Dicaboxy A-ChCl DESs. The polarity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be in the range of 1.2–0.8, while Dicarboxy A-ChCl, polarity was greater than 1. Further, the effect of hydrogen bond donors (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), KFT parameters, viscosity, fukui function of HBD, reaction time and temperature affecting the dissolution of Cu are elaborated in detail. Most dependant to least dependent parameters with respect to dissolution is recognized and some crucial conclusions were put together. Formic acid: Choline chloride (FA-ChCl) DES indicated the highest copper dissolution in the range > 10^6 ppm. Copper dissolution from ionic CuO to low polar Monocarboxy A-ChCl DESs was higher than in high polar Dicarboxy A-ChCl DESs. DFT calculation reveals that Formic Acid (FA) has the highest fukui functions compared to other carboxylic acids, which is directly reflected in the higher solubility of copper oxides. Additionally, the effect of reaction time and temperature on CuO dissolution in best-performing FA-ChCl DES was studied, 75 °C, 27 h, 100 °C, 18 h were chosen as the optimum time and temperature for maximum dissolution of Cu. The results cover important parameters of Carboxy A-ChCl DES, which could be helpful in metal extraction applications.

Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy are widely used technologies for the extraction of metals from ores and wastes such as spent catalysts and electronic wastes [11–13]. Pyrometallurgy is an intensive process that involves releasing harmful chemicals such as furan and dioxins [11]. Material loss occurs during the energy-intensive pyrometallurgical process [10]. Metals resale value and their concentration in ores or wastes play a crucial role in calculating the economic feasibility of the process. Since metal ores and urban mines are complex sources with low concentrations of metals, pyrometallurgy often rules out in terms of the economics and selectivity of metal extraction. Hydrometallurgy has been a preferred route for ores and other secondary sources with a low percentage of metals [12]. Hydrometallurgy involves the leaching of metals into a highly acidic or basic medium. However, hydrometallurgical processes discharge a colossal volume of aqueous waste into the environment during metal extraction, which should be further treated and purified before disposal [13,14] Another drawback is the occurrence of multi-metal pregnant solutions during the hydrometallurgical process due to the poor selectivity of metals. Additionally, individual pure metal is recovered using various other solvents and through a multi-step process.

In hydrometallurgy, metal extraction was conventionally done by halide leaching, acid leaching, cyanide leaching, etc., which affects the aquatic and soil ecosystem adversely [12–15]. Strong mineral acids such as HCl and H2SO4 were used in metal dissolution, with hydrogen evolution [16]. Currently, highly toxic aqua regia and cyanide solutions have been used at the industrial level, which is harmful to the environment [17]. Conventional mineral acids such as HCl, H2SO4, and HNO3 are low-cost but hold a high environmental impact after usage. Economics vs environmental factors plays a major role in the development of any process; mineral acids, though, economical have been reported to be detrimental to the environment. ILs have high thermal stability, chemical stability, and tunability, making them an excellent alternative to existing conventional solvents. However, the high cost, the complexity of synthesis methods and the debatable toxicity of ILs make them a complex media for industrialization [18,19]. Greener alternatives to hydrometallurgy and ILs should be explored for the development of more sustainable processes.

DESs are promising alternatives to ILs and traditional solvents with easy preparation and no additional purification steps. Generally, DESs are prepared by mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) with hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) at a particular ratio and a specific temperature. DES's physical properties and applications are reminiscent of ILs [20]. DESs functional groups such as carboxyl, and chlorides, which contains lone pair of electrons form metal complexes showing an efficient leaching medium [21]. DESs have been utilized in metal extraction from lithium batteries [22–25], copper ores [26], incinerated sludge [27], and NdFeB magnets [28]. The dissolution of elemental metals from waste to solution specifically in DESs is negligible without an oxidizing agent. Hence, the dissolution of metals involves an additional oxidation step with the aid of an oxidizing agent. Iodine in ethylene glycol: choline chloride DESs (EG-ChCl 2:1) has been used as a strong oxidizing power for leaching gold from gold ores [29]. Generally, organic acids are chosen as HBDs and choline chloride (ChCl) as HBA to synthesize acidic DESs. Acidic DESs, compared to mineral acids, have a moderate cost but are environmentally benign. Recovery of metals using mineral acids is significantly efficient, but the multistep precipitation and extraction are burdensome. DESs have low volatility hence can be integrated with precipitation or electrodeposition to recover metals and can be regenerated upto certain cycles [24]. Precipitation, electrodeposition and liquid–liquid extraction have been used extensively along with DESs leaching to recover metals from batteries and e-waste [24,25,30–32]. However, limited DESs as leaching agents are explored in the

literature to extract metals from metal oxides or wastes and the impact of physical properties of DESs on its application. Therefore, exhaustive research is needed to explore the role of DESs physical properties, the effect of HBDs, and several other factors on the solubility of metals in the aqueous solutions, for efficient designing of the process. The dissolution of metal oxides in choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs, prepared by varying HBDs such as ethylene glycol (EG), oxalic acid (OA), and malonic acid (MA), has been studied in the literature [33]. ChCl has been used chiefly as HBA because of its low cost, high biodegradability, and biocompatibility [34]. Commonly used HBDs are urea, carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amino acid [35]. It has been reported in the litera- ture that Carboxy A-ChCl DESs owing to their acidic properties can dissolve more metal oxides when compared to their counterparts of amide and polyol based DESs [35]. Abbott et al. compared EG-ChCl with malonic acid: choline chloride (MA-ChCl) DES and observed high metal oxide solubility in MA-ChCl [36]. The high solubility of metal was correlated with the high proton activity of solvents which accepts oxide from metal oxide, hence, breaking the bond with metals forming a chlorinated metal complex [28]. Since acidic HBD in DESs has shown promising results for metal dissolution [36,37]. Hence, for this study Carboxy A-ChCl DESs are chosen for further evaluation. Pateli et al. discussed proton activity and complexing abilities of DESs on the solu- bility of d and p block metal oxides [38]. Metal solubility in low com- plexing EG-ChCl DESs is observed to be influenced by protonation or release of H+ ions. The decrease in pH of the DESs resulted in the higher dissolution of metal oxide. In highly coordinating HBDs such as urea in urea-choline chloride (U-ChCl), surface complexation reactions have an important role in metal dissolution [38]. However, only a limited number of factors have been studied to understand the role of DESs on metal speciation.

Current research aims to compare different carboxylic acids as HBD, their effect on the physicochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs, and in the solubility of copper oxide. The effect of HBDs, HBAs, polarity, reaction temperature and reaction time of DESs on the dissolution of copper oxide was studied in detail. Copper oxides with different lattice energies of Cu(I)O (1594 kJ mol⁻¹) and Cu (II)O (4050 kJ mol⁻¹) were selected for the study [38]. Copper is a primary constituent of e-waste, worth 10,960 million USD, therefore focus is on copper dissolution [39]. Additionally, CuO has a variety of industrial applications in catalysis, solar cells due to its unique properties and versatility as a material. CuO minerals such as cuprite, azurite, malachite are also important copper source [40]. Theoretical calculations were done using density functional theory (DFT) to optimize structures and to calculate the atomic charges and fukui function of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. An intensive study on the properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs and their effect on solubility will help to better understand the green solvents and wisely utilize them in the development of metal extraction and separation processes.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Chemicals and Standards ChCl (98+%) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. FA, Acetic Acid (Acetic A), Propionic Acid (PA), Butyric Acid (BA), MA, OA, Adipic Acid (Adipic A), Succinic Acid (SA), copper(I) oxide, copper (II) oxide were obtained from Fisher Scientific. Double Distilled water with conductivity lower than 1 µS/cm was used for dilution. Reichardt dye, 4-nitroaniline, N, N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline of Alfa Aesar were used to calculate Kamlet-Taft parameters (K-T).

## 2.2. DESs preparation and analysis Highly acidic DESs with pH in the range of acidic solutions were synthesized. The synthesis temperature of 50 °C was selected for Monocarboxy A-ChCl DESs. Computational details Comprehensive and systematic analysis of these DESs was performed by DFT using Dmol³ module by Beck's three-parameter exchange functional and Lee Yang Parr correlation parameter [45]. B3LYP method was used to investigate the structures and geometrically optimize Carboxy A-ChCl DESs [46]. Density functional B3LYP is a successful method to predict accurate molecular structure and vibrational spectra in dipole-dipole forces and hydrogen bonding with lowered error [47]. To ascertain whether elements participate in organic systems as electron donors (loss) or receivers (gain), DFT simulations using fukui functions (eq. (6)-(8) have been used [48]: Nucleophilic attack $f_A^+ = q_A(N + 1) - q_A(N)$ (6) Electrophilic attack $f_A^- = q_A(N) - q_A(N - 1)$ (7) Radical attack $f_A^0 = (q_A(N + 1) - q_A(N - 1))/2$ (8) Here, $f_A$ signifies a change in the electron density of atom A when the number of electrons changes, $q_A$ represents the charge on atom A, and $(N-1)$, $N$, $(N + 1)$ signifies anionic, neutral, and cationic species, respectively.

### 2.3. Solubility of copper oxide The solubility of copper oxides in different DESs was experimentally determined. 0.2 g metal oxide was mixed with 5 mL of DES at 50 °C and 500 rpm for 24 h [36]. The solution was first centrifuged and then filtered with a syringe filter of pore size 0.2 µm. The metal concentration of the filtered sample was determined by microwave plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (MPAES) diluted with doubly distilled water. Standards of copper used are Mixture 2 of Agilent Technologies. The samples were diluted up to 1000 times to have a final metal concentration lower than 50 ppm. Triplicate experiments were conducted, and averaging was done to reach a proper conclusion.

### 3. Results and discussions #### 3.1. DES formation Monocarboxylic Acids (FA, Acetic A, PA, BA) were mixed with ChCl in 2:1 M ratio and remained liquid at room temperature. In the case of Dicarboxy A- ChCl, MA-ChCl and OA-ChCl were liquid at room temperature, while Adipic A-ChCl and SA-ChCl solidified. Dicarboxylic Acids (OA, MA, Adipic A, SA) were mixed with ChCl in 1:1 ratio. Citric acid (CA) was mixed with ChCl in 1:3 ratio.

Structural inspection of Monocarboxy A/Dicarboxy A-ChCl based DESs was analyzed using IR spectra. FTIR spectra of synthesized DES were evaluated to highlight hydrogen bonding in the eutectic systems. It was observed that the nature of HBDs and molar ratios has contributed to stretched vibrations because of a change in molecular bonding. Shifting of IR spectra of DES with respect to initial components signifies a substantial hydrogen bonding of ChCl and Monocarboxy A/Dicarboxy A. Fig. S1 (a-d) illustrates FTIR spectra of Monocarboxy A-ChCl, Dicar- boxy A-ChCl DESs.
Choline chloride have a wide band from 3621 cm-1 to 2980 cm-1 portraying presence of OH group in the vibration stretching [49].

Quaternary ammonium ion of choline chloride is represented around ~ 928–980 cm⁻¹. Vibrations for Monocarboxy A account for OH stretching, C–H stretching, sp² C–O stretching, and sp³ C–O stretching, respectively [46,50]. Shifting of OH vibration from 3027 cm⁻¹ in ChCl to 2920 cm⁻¹ in FA-ChCl indicates strong hydrogen bonding. sp² CO vibration shift was also observed in DESs, and C–H vibration shifted from 3027 to 2962 cm⁻¹. Similarly, if we consider Acetic A-ChCl, a positive shift in frequency for the C–H vibration in ChCl compared to the vibration in Acetic A-ChCl indicates the involvement of hydrogens of the methyl group in hydrogen bond formation. Shifting of the OH vibration from 3027 cm⁻¹ in ChCl to 2920 cm⁻¹ in DES indicated the formation of new hydrogen bonds. As the methyl group in HBDs increases, a greater shift in OH stretching was observed, which signifies the formation of hydrogen bonds with an increase in the H atom of a methyl group. If OH stretching of OA-ChCl and FA-ChCl are compared, there are no significant shifts in OH stretch in both acids, which signifies that the addition of COOH does not contribute much to the hydrogen bond.

Dicarboxy A-ChCl DESs have a broad band in the region of 3860 to 2270 cm⁻¹ due to OH stretching and at 1718 cm⁻¹ due to C = O stretching vibrations. C-N stretching peak of ChCl vanished in OA-ChCl, which signifies the movement of C = O under the effect of strong electronegative Cl⁻ ion. OH peak of OA-ChCl at 3392 cm⁻¹ indicates the presence of intramolecular hydrogen bonding between ChCl and OA.

3.2. *Physiochemical property of DESs* 3.2.1. *Freezing point and thermal stability* The freezing point of a eutectic mixture is a crucial parameter to estimate the magnitude of the interaction between two molecules in a binary mixture. Generally, the dip in freezing point is directly proportional to the strength of the interaction - the greater the interaction, the greater the drop in freezing point [20,35]. According to Abbott et al., for OA-ChCl eutectic mixture, the individual melting point of OA and ChCl is 101.5 °C and 302 °C, respectively [21]. However, when ChCl is mixed with OA acid at 1:1 M ratio, the freezing point of DESs was observed to be in the range of 34 °C – 30 °C in different studies [37]. The molecular weight of carboxylic acid has a significant effect on the depression of freezing point [51]. If the freezing point of an individual component is considered, much variation was observed in the literature, ChCl freezing point was in the range of 216.70 °C –302 °C [41]. Reviewing HBD freezing point, Monocarboxy A-ChCl solidifies at a lower temperature than Dicarboxy A-ChCl. DES freezing points are generally less than individual components, depending on the mole ratio (HBD:HBA) and molecular structures [39]. DESs are especially desirable when their freezing points are less than 50 °C as they will have a greater liquid range and could be used as liquid catalysts or solvents in a variety of applications [33]. The freezing point of DESs was measured using Perkin Elmer DSC 4000. Initially, 10–15 mg were placed in a nitrogen atmosphere for all samples. Heating from –20 °C to 80 °C at the rate of 5 °C/ min, equilibrating for 3 min and cooling from 80 °C to –20 °C at the rate of 1 °C/min. Table S1 illustrates the freezing point of HBD, from the above-mentioned program of DSC freezing point of PA and BA- ChCl DES cannot be determined. It was assumed to be lower than –20 °C. FA-ChCl and Acetic A-ChCl freezing points were –18.2 °C and –10.6 °C, respectively. The freezing point of Monocarboxy A-ChCl DESs has not been mentioned in the literature. The dip in freezing point of Monocarboxy A-ChCl DES is relatively less than Dicarboxy A-ChCl based DES. Hence, the hydrogen bond strength of Monocarboxy A-ChCl are relatively less as compared to Dicarboxy A-ChCl based DESs [35]. Its low freezing point is cutting edge for its wider applications in metal extraction.

3.2.2. Kamlet Taft parameter Hydrogen bond acidity (a), hydrogen basicity (β), and polarity (π) are some of the important parameters to be considered in understanding solvent properties and interactions, assisting in the prediction of DESS performance in its applications. Although, studies on KFT parameters of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs are limited [42–44,52]. Polarity measures the interactions, and ability of the solvent to alleviate charge via the dielectric effect [43]. The a depends on the cation and β on the anion part of DESS [53]. Dwamena et al. reported that polarity and acidity are independent of temperature [43]. Yet, Pandey et al. concluded that temperature does not change the polarity and basicity of DESS [42]. Florindo et al. evaluated intermolecular interactions between HBD and HBA by calculating the Kamlet Taft parameter of choline cation and carboxylic acids as anions, mainly MA-ChCl [54]. It was observed that the chemical structure of HBA and HBD have a significant effect on solvatochromic probe behaviour. Fig. 2 illustrates the calculated Kamlet Taft parameters of the synthesized DESs. Dipolarity/ polarizability of solvent (π) and hydrogen bond acidity (a) of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs decreases with an increase in alkyl chain length gesturing the prominent role of HBDs in assessing KFT parameters. ## 3.4. Mechanism The mechanism of dissolution of metals is often discussed in the literature. Abbott et al. stated that metal chlorate species are formed [MₓClO(Carboxylic acid)]⁻ in the reaction of metal with DES [21]. Carbonyl oxygen has a lone pair of electrons, it forms a coordinating bond with metal as (M—O or M—OH). However, Shishov et al. revealed carboxylic acids as the chelating agent, promoting mass transfer from metal oxides to DESs [68]. Chelate complex formation of Carboxy A-ChCl DES shows more affinity towards metal dissolution. Organic acids like OA, CA and lactic acid have been promising lixiviants for metal oxides because of the formation of complex with metals [68]. Complexation of organic anions requires two stages where first carboxyl acid is chemisorbed in the active sites of metal oxide. If the metal ligand-carboxyl complex is more stable than metal-OH, the complex anion is substituted by OH sites and the reaction is pushed forward [69]. The surface of metal oxide behaved as an electron pair donor; the system interface subsequently emerged as a positively charged layer.

## 4. Conclusion The physiochemical properties of mono/di Carboxy A-ChCl based DESs have been experimentally determined. Particularly, freezing point, thermal stability, KFT parameters of DESs were determined along with the change in density and viscosity of DESs with respect to temperatures. Monocarboxy A-ChCl based DESs were stable at room temperature, while the Dicarboxy A-ChCl remained in solid state. Density and viscosity of Dicarboxy A-ChCl was higher than Monocarboxy A-ChCl and is dependent on temperature. Among all considered DESs, FA-ChCl have lowest viscosity and density as compared to other Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. The solubility of Cu (I)O and Cu (II)O was observed to be highest in FA-ChCl (greater than 10⁶ ppm) which decreases with an increase in alkyl chain length of HBD of DES. CuO dissolution in DES was observed to be independent of polarity of solvent as it was observed to be dissolved more in FA-ChCl than higher polar OA-ChCl. Effect of time and temperature on copper dissolution was evaluated in best-performing FA-ChCl DESs. 100 °C, 18 h or 75 °C, 27 h were optimum condition for maximum copper dissolution. Results of this paper focuses on detailed physiochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can directly be utilized to predict DESs performance in various industrial applications. It covers critical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can play a significant role in solubility of metals or gases in Carboxy A-ChCl DES. Moreover, mechanism of metal DESs interaction is still lacking in the literature. Theoretical studies could be combined with experimental results to interrogate molecular level interaction of DESs with metals for future studies. Pant⁰,*, Bhoopesh Mishraⁱ a Green and Sustainable Engineering Lab, Department of Chemical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, India b Illinois Institute of Technology, Chicago, IL, United States ARTICLE INFO --- *Keywords:* Deep eutectic solvents Metal leaching DFT Green solvent Oxides ## A B S T R A C T Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are green alternatives to highly acidic solvents or ionic liquids (ILs). The flexible complexation properties of eutectic solvents open their scope as a prospective dissolution medium for metal extraction. The present study investigates the range of monocarboxylic acids-choline chloride (Monocarboxy A-ChCl) and dicarboxylic acid-choline chloride (Dicarboxy A-ChCl) DESs as solvent media for copper oxide dissolution with a discussion on physical properties and their effect on dissolution. Thermal stability, freezing point, Kamlet Taft parameter, density, and viscosity of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs were experimentally determined. The density of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs follows the trend: FA-ChCl < Acetic A-ChCl < OA-ChCl < MA-ChCl < CA-ChCl. The viscosity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be lesser than Dicaboxy A-ChCl DESs. The polarity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be in the range of 1.2–0.8, while Dicarboxy A-ChCl, polarity was greater than 1. Further, the effect of hydrogen bond donors (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), KFT parameters, viscosity, fukui function of HBD, reaction time and temperature affecting the dissolution of Cu are elaborated in detail. Most dependant to least dependent parameters with respect to dissolution is recognized and some crucial conclusions were put together. Formic acid: Choline chloride (FA-ChCl) DES indicated the highest copper dissolution in the range > 10^6 ppm. Copper dissolution from ionic CuO to low polar Monocarboxy A-ChCl DESs was higher than in high polar Dicarboxy A-ChCl DESs. DFT calculation reveals that Formic Acid (FA) has the highest fukui functions compared to other carboxylic acids, which is directly reflected in the higher solubility of copper oxides. Additionally, the effect of reaction time and temperature on CuO dissolution in best-performing FA-ChCl DES was studied, 75 °C, 27 h, 100 °C, 18 h were chosen as the optimum time and temperature for maximum dissolution of Cu. The results cover important parameters of Carboxy A-ChCl DES, which could be helpful in metal extraction applications. ## 1. Introduction Metal oxides exist naturally in the form of mineral ores such as hematite (Fe2O3), cuprite (Cu2O), and pyrolusite (MnO2). It is also in high composition in several waste materials such as lithium-ion batteries [1,2], spent catalysts [3-6], and as mining industry residues in the form of dust particles [7], slag [8], etc. Dissolution of metals has wide application during etching in the microelectronics industry, surface polishing of metals, synthesis of organometallic compounds, and extraction of metals from their ores [9]. Recy- cling metals from these wastes is an urgent necessity to reduce the burn on mining industries and minimize the environmental effects. Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy are widely used technologies for the extraction of metals from ores and wastes such as spent catalysts and electronic wastes [11–13]. Pyrometallurgy is an intensive process that involves releasing harmful chemicals such as furan and dioxins [11]. Material loss occurs during the energy-intensive pyrometallurgical process [10]. Metals resale value and their concentration in ores or wastes play a crucial role in calculating the economic feasibility of the process. Since metal ores and urban mines are complex sources with low concentrations of metals, pyrometallurgy often rules out in terms of the economics and selectivity of metal extraction. Hydrometallurgy has been a preferred route for ores and other secondary sources with a low percentage of metals [12]. Hydrometallurgy involves the leaching of metals into a highly acidic or basic medium. However, hydrometallurgical processes discharge a colossal volume of aqueous waste into the environment during metal extraction, which should be further treated and purified before disposal [13,14] Another drawback is the occurrence of multi-metal pregnant solutions during the hydrometallurgical process due to the poor selectivity of metals. Additionally, individual pure metal is recovered using various other solvents and through a multi-step process. In hydrometallurgy, metal extraction was conventionally done by halide leaching, acid leaching, cyanide leaching, etc., which affects the aquatic and soil ecosystem adversely [12–15]. Strong mineral acids such as HCl and H2SO4 were used in metal dissolution, with hydrogen evolution [16]. Currently, highly toxic aqua regia and cyanide solutions have been used at the industrial level, which is harmful to the environment [17]. Conventional mineral acids such as HCl, H2SO4, and HNO3 are low-cost but hold a high environmental impact after usage. Economics vs environmental factors plays a major role in the development of any process; mineral acids, though, economical have been reported to be detrimental to the environment. ILs have high thermal stability, chemical stability, and tunability, making them an excellent alternative to existing conventional solvents. However, the high cost, the complexity of synthesis methods and the debatable toxicity of ILs make them a complex media for industrialization [18,19]. Greener alternatives to hydrometallurgy and ILs should be explored for the development of more sustainable processes. DESs are promising alternatives to ILs and traditional solvents with easy preparation and no additional purification steps. Generally, DESs are prepared by mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) with hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) at a particular ratio and a specific temperature. DES's physical properties and applications are reminiscent of ILs [20]. DESs functional groups such as carboxyl, and chlorides, which contains lone pair of electrons form metal complexes showing an efficient leaching medium [21]. DESs have been utilized in metal extraction from lithium batteries [22–25], copper ores [26], incinerated sludge [27], and NdFeB magnets [28]. The dissolution of elemental metals from waste to solution specifically in DESs is negligible without an oxidizing agent. Hence, the dissolution of metals involves an additional oxidation step with the aid of an oxidizing agent. Iodine in ethylene glycol: choline chloride DESs (EG-ChCl 2:1) has been used as a strong oxidizing power for leaching gold from gold ores [29]. Generally, organic acids are chosen as HBDs and choline chloride (ChCl) as HBA to synthesize acidic DESs. Acidic DESs, compared to mineral acids, have a moderate cost but are environmentally benign. Recovery of metals using mineral acids is significantly efficient, but the multistep precipitation and extraction are burdensome. DESs have low volatility hence can be integrated with precipitation or electrodeposition to recover metals and can be regenerated upto certain cycles [24]. Precipitation, electrodeposition and liquid–liquid extraction have been used extensively along with DESs leaching to recover metals from batteries and e-waste [24,25,30–32]. However, limited DESs as leaching agents are explored in the literature to extract metals from metal oxides or wastes and the impact of physical properties of DESs on its application. Therefore, exhaustive research is needed to explore the role of DESs physical properties, the effect of HBDs, and several other factors on the solubility of metals in the aqueous solutions, for efficient designing of the process. The dissolution of metal oxides in choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs, prepared by varying HBDs such as ethylene glycol (EG), oxalic acid (OA), and malonic acid (MA), has been studied in the literature [33]. ChCl has been used chiefly as HBA because of its low cost, high biodegradability, and biocompatibility [34]. Commonly used HBDs are urea, carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amino acid [35]. It has been reported in the litera- ture that Carboxy A-ChCl DESs owing to their acidic properties can dissolve more metal oxides when compared to their counterparts of amide and polyol based DESs [35]. Abbott et al. compared EG-ChCl with malonic acid: choline chloride (MA-ChCl) DES and observed high metal oxide solubility in MA-ChCl [36]. The high solubility of metal was correlated with the high proton activity of solvents which accepts oxide from metal oxide, hence, breaking the bond with metals forming a chlorinated metal complex [28]. Since acidic HBD in DESs has shown promising results for metal dissolution [36,37]. Hence, for this study Carboxy A-ChCl DESs are chosen for further evaluation. Pateli et al. discussed proton activity and complexing abilities of DESs on the solu- bility of d and p block metal oxides [38]. Metal solubility in low com- plexing EG-ChCl DESs is observed to be influenced by protonation or release of H+ ions. The decrease in pH of the DESs resulted in the higher dissolution of metal oxide. In highly coordinating HBDs such as urea in urea-choline chloride (U-ChCl), surface complexation reactions have an important role in metal dissolution [38]. However, only a limited number of factors have been studied to understand the role of DESs on metal speciation. Current research aims to compare different carboxylic acids as HBD, their effect on the physicochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs, and in the solubility of copper oxide. The effect of HBDs, HBAs, polarity, reaction temperature and reaction time of DESs on the dissolution of copper oxide was studied in detail. Copper oxides with different lattice energies of Cu(I)O (1594 kJ mol⁻¹) and Cu (II)O (4050 kJ mol⁻¹) were selected for the study [38]. Copper is a primary constituent of e-waste, worth 10,960 million USD, therefore focus is on copper dissolution [39]. Additionally, CuO has a variety of industrial applications in catalysis, solar cells due to its unique properties and versatility as a material. CuO minerals such as cuprite, azurite, malachite are also important copper source [40]. Theoretical calculations were done using density functional theory (DFT) to optimize structures and to calculate the atomic charges and fukui function of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. An intensive study on the properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs and their effect on solubility will help to better understand the green solvents and wisely utilize them in the development of metal extraction and separation processes. ## 2. Mechanism The mechanism of dissolution of metals is often discussed in the literature. Abbott et al. stated that metal chlorate species are formed [MₓClO(Carboxylic acid)]⁻ in the reaction of metal with DES [21]. Carbonyl oxygen has a lone pair of electrons, it forms a coordinating bond with metal as (M—O or M—OH). However, Shishov et al. revealed carboxylic acids as the chelating agent, promoting mass transfer from metal oxides to DESs [68]. Chelate complex formation of Carboxy A-ChCl DES shows more affinity towards metal dissolution. Organic acids like OA, CA and lactic acid have been promising lixiviants for metal oxides because of the formation of complex with metals [68]. Complexation of organic anions requires two stages where first carboxyl acid is chemisorbed in the active sites of metal oxide. If the metal ligand-carboxyl complex is more stable than metal-OH, the complex anion is substituted by OH sites and the reaction is pushed forward [69]. The surface of metal oxide behaved as an electron pair donor; the system interface subsequently emerged as a positively charged layer. Particularly, freezing point, thermal stability, KFT parameters of DESs were determined along with the change in density and viscosity of DESs with respect to temperatures. Monocarboxy A-ChCl based DESs were stable at room temperature, while the Dicarboxy A-ChCl remained in solid state. Density and viscosity of Dicarboxy A-ChCl was higher than Monocarboxy A-ChCl and is dependent on temperature. Among all considered DESs, FA-ChCl have lowest viscosity and density as compared to other Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. The solubility of Cu (I)O and Cu (II)O was observed to be highest in FA-ChCl (greater than 10⁶ ppm) which decreases with an increase in alkyl chain length of HBD of DES. CuO dissolution in DES was observed to be independent of polarity of solvent as it was observed to be dissolved more in FA-ChCl than higher polar OA-ChCl. Effect of time and temperature on copper dissolution was evaluated in best-performing FA-ChCl DESs. 100 °C, 18 h or 75 °C, 27 h were optimum condition for maximum copper dissolution. Results of this paper focuses on detailed physiochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can directly be utilized to predict DESs performance in various industrial applications. It covers critical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can play a significant role in solubility of metals or gases in Carboxy A-ChCl DES. Moreover, mechanism of metal DESs interaction is still lacking in the literature. Theoretical studies could be combined with experimental results to interrogate molecular level interaction of DESs with metals for future studies. Pant⁰,*, Bhoopesh Mishraⁱ a Green and Sustainable Engineering Lab, Department of Chemical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, India b Illinois Institute of Technology, Chicago, IL, United States ARTICLE INFO --- *Keywords:* Deep eutectic solvents Metal leaching DFT Green solvent Oxides ## A B S T R A C T Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are green alternatives to highly acidic solvents or ionic liquids (ILs). The flexible complexation properties of eutectic solvents open their scope as a prospective dissolution medium for metal extraction. The present study investigates the range of monocarboxylic acids-choline chloride (Monocarboxy A-ChCl) and dicarboxylic acid-choline chloride (Dicarboxy A-ChCl) DESs as solvent media for copper oxide dissolution with a discussion on physical properties and their effect on dissolution. Thermal stability, freezing point, Kamlet Taft parameter, density, and viscosity of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs were experimentally determined. The density of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs follows the trend: FA-ChCl < Acetic A-ChCl < OA-ChCl < MA-ChCl < CA-ChCl. The viscosity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be lesser than Dicaboxy A-ChCl DESs. The polarity of Monocarboxy A-ChCl was observed to be in the range of 1.2–0.8, while Dicarboxy A-ChCl, polarity was greater than 1. Further, the effect of hydrogen bond donors (HBD), hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA), KFT parameters, viscosity, fukui function of HBD, reaction time and temperature affecting the dissolution of Cu are elaborated in detail. Most dependant to least dependent parameters with respect to dissolution is recognized and some crucial conclusions were put together. Formic acid: Choline chloride (FA-ChCl) DES indicated the highest copper dissolution in the range > 10^6 ppm. Copper dissolution from ionic CuO to low polar Monocarboxy A-ChCl DESs was higher than in high polar Dicarboxy A-ChCl DESs. DFT calculation reveals that Formic Acid (FA) has the highest fukui functions compared to other carboxylic acids, which is directly reflected in the higher solubility of copper oxides. Additionally, the effect of reaction time and temperature on CuO dissolution in best-performing FA-ChCl DES was studied, 75 °C, 27 h, 100 °C, 18 h were chosen as the optimum time and temperature for maximum dissolution of Cu. The results cover important parameters of Carboxy A-ChCl DES, which could be helpful in metal extraction applications. ## 1. Introduction Metal oxides exist naturally in the form of mineral ores such as hematite (Fe2O3), cuprite (Cu2O), and pyrolusite (MnO2). It is also in high composition in several waste materials such as lithium-ion batteries [1,2], spent catalysts [3-6], and as mining industry residues in the form of dust particles [7], slag [8], etc. Dissolution of metals has wide application during etching in the microelectronics industry, surface polishing of metals, synthesis of organometallic compounds, and extraction of metals from their ores [9]. Recy- cling metals from these wastes is an urgent necessity to reduce the burn on mining industries and minimize the environmental effects. Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy are widely used technologies for the extraction of metals from ores and wastes such as spent catalysts and electronic wastes [11–13]. Pyrometallurgy is an intensive process that involves releasing harmful chemicals such as furan and dioxins [11]. Material loss occurs during the energy-intensive pyrometallurgical process [10]. Metals resale value and their concentration in ores or wastes play a crucial role in calculating the economic feasibility of the process. Since metal ores and urban mines are complex sources with low concentrations of metals, pyrometallurgy often rules out in terms of the economics and selectivity of metal extraction. Hydrometallurgy has been a preferred route for ores and other secondary sources with a low percentage of metals [12]. Hydrometallurgy involves the leaching of metals into a highly acidic or basic medium. However, hydrometallurgical processes discharge a colossal volume of aqueous waste into the environment during metal extraction, which should be further treated and purified before disposal [13,14] Another drawback is the occurrence of multi-metal pregnant solutions during the hydrometallurgical process due to the poor selectivity of metals. Additionally, individual pure metal is recovered using various other solvents and through a multi-step process. In hydrometallurgy, metal extraction was conventionally done by halide leaching, acid leaching, cyanide leaching, etc., which affects the aquatic and soil ecosystem adversely [12–15]. Strong mineral acids such as HCl and H2SO4 were used in metal dissolution, with hydrogen evolution [16]. Currently, highly toxic aqua regia and cyanide solutions have been used at the industrial level, which is harmful to the environment [17]. Conventional mineral acids such as HCl, H2SO4, and HNO3 are low-cost but hold a high environmental impact after usage. Economics vs environmental factors plays a major role in the development of any process; mineral acids, though, economical have been reported to be detrimental to the environment. ILs have high thermal stability, chemical stability, and tunability, making them an excellent alternative to existing conventional solvents. However, the high cost, the complexity of synthesis methods and the debatable toxicity of ILs make them a complex media for industrialization [18,19]. Greener alternatives to hydrometallurgy and ILs should be explored for the development of more sustainable processes. DESs are promising alternatives to ILs and traditional solvents with easy preparation and no additional purification steps. Generally, DESs are prepared by mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) with hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) at a particular ratio and a specific temperature. DES's physical properties and applications are reminiscent of ILs [20]. DESs functional groups such as carboxyl, and chlorides, which contains lone pair of electrons form metal complexes showing an efficient leaching medium [21]. DESs have been utilized in metal extraction from lithium batteries [22–25], copper ores [26], incinerated sludge [27], and NdFeB magnets [28]. The dissolution of elemental metals from waste to solution specifically in DESs is negligible without an oxidizing agent. Hence, the dissolution of metals involves an additional oxidation step with the aid of an oxidizing agent. Iodine in ethylene glycol: choline chloride DESs (EG-ChCl 2:1) has been used as a strong oxidizing power for leaching gold from gold ores [29]. Generally, organic acids are chosen as HBDs and choline chloride (ChCl) as HBA to synthesize acidic DESs. Acidic DESs, compared to mineral acids, have a moderate cost but are environmentally benign. Recovery of metals using mineral acids is significantly efficient, but the multistep precipitation and extraction are burdensome. DESs have low volatility hence can be integrated with precipitation or electrodeposition to recover metals and can be regenerated upto certain cycles [24]. Precipitation, electrodeposition and liquid–liquid extraction have been used extensively along with DESs leaching to recover metals from batteries and e-waste [24,25,30–32]. However, limited DESs as leaching agents are explored in the literature to extract metals from metal oxides or wastes and the impact of physical properties of DESs on its application. Therefore, exhaustive research is needed to explore the role of DESs physical properties, the effect of HBDs, and several other factors on the solubility of metals in the aqueous solutions, for efficient designing of the process. The dissolution of metal oxides in choline chloride (ChCl)-based DESs, prepared by varying HBDs such as ethylene glycol (EG), oxalic acid (OA), and malonic acid (MA), has been studied in the literature [33]. ChCl has been used chiefly as HBA because of its low cost, high biodegradability, and biocompatibility [34]. Commonly used HBDs are urea, carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amino acid [35]. It has been reported in the litera- ture that Carboxy A-ChCl DESs owing to their acidic properties can dissolve more metal oxides when compared to their counterparts of amide and polyol based DESs [35]. Abbott et al. compared EG-ChCl with malonic acid: choline chloride (MA-ChCl) DES and observed high metal oxide solubility in MA-ChCl [36]. The high solubility of metal was correlated with the high proton activity of solvents which accepts oxide from metal oxide, hence, breaking the bond with metals forming a chlorinated metal complex [28]. Since acidic HBD in DESs has shown promising results for metal dissolution [36,37]. Hence, for this study Carboxy A-ChCl DESs are chosen for further evaluation. Pateli et al. discussed proton activity and complexing abilities of DESs on the solu- bility of d and p block metal oxides [38]. Metal solubility in low com- plexing EG-ChCl DESs is observed to be influenced by protonation or release of H+ ions. The decrease in pH of the DESs resulted in the higher dissolution of metal oxide. In highly coordinating HBDs such as urea in urea-choline chloride (U-ChCl), surface complexation reactions have an important role in metal dissolution [38]. However, only a limited number of factors have been studied to understand the role of DESs on metal speciation. Current research aims to compare different carboxylic acids as HBD, their effect on the physicochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs, and in the solubility of copper oxide. The effect of HBDs, HBAs, polarity, reaction temperature and reaction time of DESs on the dissolution of copper oxide was studied in detail. Copper oxides with different lattice energies of Cu(I)O (1594 kJ mol⁻¹) and Cu (II)O (4050 kJ mol⁻¹) were selected for the study [38]. Copper is a primary constituent of e-waste, worth 10,960 million USD, therefore focus is on copper dissolution [39]. Additionally, CuO has a variety of industrial applications in catalysis, solar cells due to its unique properties and versatility as a material. CuO minerals such as cuprite, azurite, malachite are also important copper source [40]. Theoretical calculations were done using density functional theory (DFT) to optimize structures and to calculate the atomic charges and fukui function of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. An intensive study on the properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DESs and their effect on solubility will help to better understand the green solvents and wisely utilize them in the development of metal extraction and separation processes. ## 2. Mechanism The mechanism of dissolution of metals is often discussed in the literature. Abbott et al. stated that metal chlorate species are formed [MₓClO(Carboxylic acid)]⁻ in the reaction of metal with DES [21]. Carbonyl oxygen has a lone pair of electrons, it forms a coordinating bond with metal as (M—O or M—OH). However, Shishov et al. revealed carboxylic acids as the chelating agent, promoting mass transfer from metal oxides to DESs [68]. Chelate complex formation of Carboxy A-ChCl DES shows more affinity towards metal dissolution. Organic acids like OA, CA and lactic acid have been promising lixiviants for metal oxides because of the formation of complex with metals [68]. Complexation of organic anions requires two stages where first carboxyl acid is chemisorbed in the active sites of metal oxide. If the metal ligand-carboxyl complex is more stable than metal-OH, the complex anion is substituted by OH sites and the reaction is pushed forward [69]. The surface of metal oxide behaved as an electron pair donor; the system interface subsequently emerged as a positively charged layer. Particularly, freezing point, thermal stability, KFT parameters of DESs were determined along with the change in density and viscosity of DESs with respect to temperatures. Monocarboxy A-ChCl based DESs were stable at room temperature, while the Dicarboxy A-ChCl remained in solid state. Density and viscosity of Dicarboxy A-ChCl was higher than Monocarboxy A-ChCl and is dependent on temperature. Among all considered DESs, FA-ChCl have lowest viscosity and density as compared to other Carboxy A-ChCl DESs. The solubility of Cu (I)O and Cu (II)O was observed to be highest in FA-ChCl (greater than 10⁶ ppm) which decreases with an increase in alkyl chain length of HBD of DES. CuO dissolution in DES was observed to be independent of polarity of solvent as it was observed to be dissolved more in FA-ChCl than higher polar OA-ChCl. Effect of time and temperature on copper dissolution was evaluated in best-performing FA-ChCl DESs. 100 °C, 18 h or 75 °C, 27 h were optimum condition for maximum copper dissolution. Results of this paper focuses on detailed physiochemical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can directly be utilized to predict DESs performance in various industrial applications. It covers critical properties of Carboxy A-ChCl DES which can play a significant role in solubility of metals or gases in Carboxy A-ChCl DES. Moreover, mechanism of metal DESs interaction is still lacking in the literature. Theoretical studies could be combined with experimental results to interrogate molecular level interaction of DESs with metals for future studies.
